The Secretary’s practice of counting a single, nonrecurring "gate release" payment to reduce benefits across three consecutive months violates the plain language and intent of 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c). The statute mandates that benefit determinations in the initial month of eligibility be based on the "relevant circumstances" of the beneficiary. The defining and most "relevant" characteristic of a one-time release payment is precisely that it is nonrecurring—it is available only once to meet immediate subsistence needs.

By utilizing this single sum to reduce benefits in the first month, the second month, and again in the third month via the Retrospective Monthly Accounting (RMA) look-back, the Secretary creates a punishing legal fiction. This approach treats a one-time lifeline as a recurring income stream, resulting in a "triple deduction" that leaves destitute individuals without necessary support. The transitional exception in the statute was designed to ensure accuracy when a beneficiary re-enters the system, not to create a bureaucratic trap where the mechanics of accounting override the reality of financial need.

To be faithful to the statutory requirement of assessing "relevant circumstances," the Secretary must acknowledge the nonrecurring nature of this income. Congress intended the transitional rules to bridge the gap between actual need and the RMA system, not to artificially inflate a beneficiary's income. A calculation method that ignores the factual reality that the money was received only once is arbitrary, capricious, and inconsistent with the program's benevolent purpose. The Carter Class must prevail to ensure that benefit calculations reflect actual economic reality rather than administrative convenience.

The Carter Class must prevail because the Secretary’s application of Retrospective Monthly Accounting (RMA) violates the statutory mandate to consider "relevant circumstances" under 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c)(5). By counting a single, non-recurring "gate release" payment against benefits in three separate months, the Secretary creates a punitive fiction that the beneficiary possesses income they do not actually have.

The statute governs the "transitional computation cycle" to accurately assess a newly eligible individual’s immediate financial reality. Section 1382(c)(5) explicitly authorizes the Secretary to prescribe criteria based on "relevant circumstances." The definitive "relevant circumstance" of a one-time gate release payment is its *non-recurring nature*. By ignoring this characteristic, the Secretary’s rigid formula effectively assumes Mr. Carter received that income three times.

Furthermore, the purpose of the prospective accounting exception in the first month is to align benefits with actual current need. When the Secretary allows that same income to trigger subsequent reductions under the two-month look-back rule, it nullifies the statutory protection intended for new beneficiaries. This creates an absurdity where a subsistence-level benefit is slashed based on funds already exhausted on immediate post-detention survival.

The Court should reject this "triple deduction" anomaly. A faithful interpretation of 42 U.S.C. § 1382 requires that non-recurring income be counted only once—during the month it is received—to ensure the program fulfills its Congressional purpose: providing for the actual, current needs of the vulnerable.

The Secretary’s practice of triple-counting a single, nonrecurring payment violates the plain text and humanitarian purpose of 42 U.S.C. § 1382. Under Section 1382(c)(5), the calculation for the initial month of eligibility must rely on income and "other relevant circumstances." The most "relevant circumstance" regarding Mr. Carter’s gate-release payment is that it was a one-time event, not a continuing revenue stream.

By mechanically applying this single payment to reduce benefits in the first two "transitional" months and again in the third month via Retrospective Monthly Accounting, the Secretary creates a legal fiction that the beneficiary possesses income they do not actually have. This approach ignores the statutory mandate to assess the "actual" economic reality of the beneficiary during the transitional period.

Congress intended the specific exception for initial eligibility to ensure that benefits match current needs. The Secretary’s policy subverts this intent by transforming a meager start-up fund into a three-month penalty. If the statute requires looking at "relevant circumstances," the agency cannot legally ignore the dispositive fact that the income has ceased. To hold otherwise allows an administrative accounting rule to defeat the substantive statutory right to subsistence benefits. The Carter Class asks this Court to enforce the statute’s requirement for accuracy over the Agency’s preference for administrative convenience.

The Carter Class must prevail because the Secretary’s “triple-deduction” policy violates both the plain text and the remedial purpose of 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c). While the statute generally establishes Retrospective Monthly Accounting (RMA), § 1382(c)(2)(A) explicitly requires that, for the first month of eligibility, benefit determination must be based on the “relevant circumstances” of that month.

The definition of “relevant circumstances” is the linchpin of this dispute. The most relevant characteristic of a gate-release payment is its *nonrecurring* nature. By definition, this income exists only at the moment of release. When the Secretary utilizes this single payment to reduce benefits in the first month (prospectively) and then again in the second and third months (retrospectively), the agency willfully ignores the factual reality that the income has ceased.

Furthermore, § 1382(c)(5) authorizes the Secretary to rely on information only when it is “reliable.” Treating a one-time payment as a recurring revenue stream for three consecutive months is inherently unreliable and arbitrary. This bureaucratic mechanic effectively imputes income to Mr. Carter that he does not possess, forcing a destitute individual to stretch a single month’s worth of emergency funds across a quarter of a year.

Congress intended these benefits to provide a subsistence floor for the needy. A calculation method that artificially inflates a beneficiary's income by triple-counting a single payment defeats this statutory intent. To comply with the mandate to consider “relevant circumstances,” the Court must rule that nonrecurring income may legally be counted only once.

The Carter Class must prevail because the Secretary’s rigid application of Retrospective Monthly Accounting (RMA) to nonrecurring income violates the statutory mandate to assess "relevant circumstances" under 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c)(2)(A).

The central flaw in the Secretary’s policy is the failure to recognize that the cessation of a one-time payment is a critical "relevant circumstance." When Andrew Carter received a single "gate release" payment, that income was finite. Yet, the Secretary’s method deducted this amount from the first month’s benefit (prospectively), and then utilized the retrospective look-back mechanism to deduct that *same* amount again in subsequent months. This creates a punitive "triple-deduction" scenario where a beneficiary is penalized multiple times for a single instance of financial support.

While 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c)(5) allows the Secretary discretion regarding the second month, this discretion cannot override the requirement to base the initial month's eligibility on actual circumstances. By mechanically applying the first month’s income to determine the third month’s benefit—despite knowing that income was a one-off event—the Secretary artificially inflates the beneficiary's perceived financial resources.

The statute was designed to assist those in need, not to create a bureaucratic trap where a one-time lifeline results in three months of reduced subsistence. To be faithful to the text, "relevant circumstances" must include the nonrecurring nature of the income. Therefore, the Court should hold that the statute prohibits counting nonrecurring initial income in subsequent monthly calculations, ensuring that benefit reductions correspond to the beneficiary's actual ability to pay.

The Secretary’s benefit calculation must be upheld because it adheres strictly to the statutory framework mandated by Congress in 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c). The statute establishes a general rule of Retrospective Monthly Accounting (RMA), requiring that benefits be calculated based on income received in the second preceding month. While the statute provides a necessary exception for the first month of eligibility—using current income to determine immediate need—it does not exempt that initial income from the standard RMA look-back mechanism required for subsequent months.

The Secretary’s policy is not an arbitrary "triple deduction," but rather the faithful execution of two distinct statutory directives: the transitional calculation (prospective) and the standard calculation (retrospective). When calculating the benefit for Month 3, the statute explicitly commands the Secretary to look back at the income received in Month 1. The fact that this income was "nonrecurring" does not erase its existence during the statutorily defined look-back period. To exclude this income from the Month 3 calculation would require the Secretary to violate the clear statutory command to base payments on the second preceding month’s income.

Furthermore, the "relevant circumstances" provision in § 1382(c)(5) grants the Secretary discretion to verify eligibility, not to rewrite the mechanical operation of the RMA cycle. The recurrence of the income data in the calculation is a mathematical consequence of the Congressional design of RMA, which prioritizes administrative consistency. The Secretary’s detailed guidance reasonably bridges the gap between initial eligibility and the ongoing retrospective system; overturning this interpretation would effectively force the agency to ignore actual income received, contradicting the program's means-tested nature.

The Secretary should prevail because the benefit calculations strictly adhere to the statutory mandates of the Retrospective Monthly Accounting (RMA) system established by Congress.

First, 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c) requires a "transitional computation" for new entrants, basing the initial month's benefit on actual, current income to ensure immediate accuracy. Second, the statute mandates that subsequent benefits be calculated based on income from the second preceding month.

There is no statutory provision that forbids income counted in the initial prospective month from being utilized later in the standard retrospective calculation. The "gate release" payment was actual income received in the first month. Therefore, it is legally required to factor into the first month’s calculation (as current income) and the third month’s calculation (as historical income under the two-month look-back rule).

To adopt the Carter Class’s position would require the Secretary to arbitrarily ignore actual income received during the look-back period, violating the core statutory requirement of RMA. The fact that the income was nonrecurring does not erase its existence during the relevant accounting periods. The Secretary’s detailed guidance reasonably interprets this complex statutory scheme by applying the plain text of the accounting rules mechanically. Because the Secretary’s policy faithfully executes the interaction between initial eligibility rules and mandatory retrospective accounting without an explicit statutory exception for nonrecurring income, the Court must uphold the Secretary’s interpretation.

The Secretary’s policy constitutes a faithful and necessary application of the statutory framework mandated by Congress. The governing statute, 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c), explicitly establishes Retrospective Monthly Accounting (RMA) as the standard mechanism for benefit calculation. Under RMA, the benefit amount for a specific month is statutorily defined by the income received in the second preceding month.

While the statute provides a transitional exception—allowing prospective calculation for the first two months to facilitate immediate aid—it clearly dictates a revert to the RMA system by the third month. Consequently, when calculating the benefit for Month 3, the Secretary is legally compelled to look back at the income received in Month 1. That the Month 1 income was also used to calculate Month 1 benefits is not an error, but the mechanical result of the statutory shift from prospective to retrospective accounting.

The Carter Class's argument regarding "relevant circumstances" asks the Court to prioritize a vague catch-all phrase over the specific, rigid formula provided by the RMA provision. The statute does not contain an exclusion for "nonrecurring income" within the RMA look-back; it simply commands the Secretary to count the income from the second prior month. To ignore the gate-release payment in the Month 3 calculation would require the Secretary to violate the express terms of the RMA mandate.

Therefore, the Secretary’s approach avoids arbitrary administrative discretion and strictly adheres to the text of the Act. The perceived "triple deduction" is simply the lawful consequence of Congress’s decision to mandate two distinct accounting methodologies that inevitably overlap during the transitional period.

The Secretary’s calculation method is a faithful application of the unambiguous statutory text found in 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c). The statute creates two distinct, mandatory frameworks for calculating benefits: a prospective method for initial eligibility and a Retrospective Monthly Accounting (RMA) system for ongoing benefits.

For the initial month, the statute explicitly requires a prospective calculation based on actual income to assess immediate need. Mr. Carter possessed income in that first month; therefore, the Secretary was legally obligated to count it. For the third month and beyond, the statute mandates RMA, requiring benefits to be calculated based on income received in the second preceding month. Consequently, when calculating the third month’s benefit, the Secretary is statutorily compelled to look back at the income received in the first month.

The Carter Class characterizes this as an unfair policy choice, but it is actually the mechanical result of complying with two independent statutory directives. The “relevant circumstances” provision cited by the plaintiffs permits the Secretary to assess eligibility factors, but it does not grant the authority to ignore the specific Congressional mandate to utilize RMA. To exclude the initial payment from the third month’s calculation would require the Secretary to arbitrarily ignore the clear statutory instruction to base payments on the second preceding month's income.

The Secretary’s regulations simply harmonize these two statutory commands. Because the agency’s approach adheres strictly to the text of the Act by accurately reflecting income in the specific months the statute designates for calculation, the Secretary’s policy must be upheld.

The Secretary’s application of the "transitional computation cycle" adheres strictly to the statutory text. Congress mandated two distinct accounting methods: prospective accounting for the initial month of eligibility under 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c)(2)(A), and Retrospective Monthly Accounting (RMA) for ongoing benefits. The Secretary has faithfully applied both directives.

The "triple deduction" described by the Carter Class is not an arbitrary agency penalty, but the mechanical result of the statutory transition. For the first month, the Secretary must consider current income to determine immediate need. For the third month, the statute explicitly commands the Secretary to determine benefits based on income received in the second preceding month. Andrew Carter undeniably received income in that first month. To ignore that income during the Month 3 calculation would violate the statutory mandate to look back at Month 1.

Furthermore, the plaintiffs misapply the "relevant circumstances" provision of § 1382(c)(2)(A). This provision directs the Secretary to assess the reliability of information for the *initial* prospective month; it is not a license to ignore actual financial facts during the subsequent RMA calculations. The nonrecurring nature of the payment does not change the historical fact that the funds were available to the beneficiary in Month 1.

The Secretary’s policy is the only interpretation that harmonizes the conflicting statutory requirements: it accounts for immediate need upon release while establishing the statutory look-back period required for ongoing administration. Because the Secretary’s approach relies on the actual receipt of income and strictly follows the retrospective formula mandated by Congress, the Court should uphold the policy.

The Court must deny Davidson’s motion to compel arbitration because arbitration is strictly a matter of consent, not coercion. Davidson is a non-signatory to the agreement between Harper Investors and Gold Reserve & Lending. Under the Federal Arbitration Act, a party cannot be required to submit to arbitration any dispute which they have not agreed so to submit.

Davidson’s attempt to enforce the clause via agency or equitable estoppel fails because Harper’s claims are not integrally linked to the underlying contract. Instead, the allegations stem from Davidson’s independent, subsequent tortious conduct. Davidson utilized separate entities—Fund Restoration Alliance and Tax Support Circle—to solicit funds and fraudulently induce investors to forgo legal action. These acts occurred after the original contract was executed and fall outside the scope of the Gold Reserve agreement.

By operating through these independent entities to perpetrate fraud, Davidson acted outside his capacity as an agent of Gold Reserve. He effectively severed the nexus between his conduct and the original investment agreement. Permitting Davidson to compel arbitration would allow a non-signatory to weaponize a contract he never signed to shield himself from liability for personal, independent fraud. Because the dispute arises from Davidson’s specific misconduct rather than the interpretation of the Gold Reserve contract, he lacks standing to enforce the arbitration clause.

The Court must deny Jon Davidson’s motion to compel arbitration because arbitration is strictly a matter of consent, not coercion. Harper Investors never agreed to arbitrate disputes with Davidson, a non-signatory who inserted himself into the scheme long after the original agreements with Gold Reserve & Lending were executed.

While federal policy favors arbitration, it does not permit a non-signatory to highjack a contract to shield independent tortious conduct. For a non-signatory to compel arbitration under equitable estoppel, the plaintiff’s claims must rely on the terms of the written agreement. That is not the case here. Harper Investors’ claims against Davidson do not arise from the breach of the original Gold Reserve contract terms, but rather from Davidson’s subsequent, independent acts of fraud and solicitation.

Davidson utilized entirely separate entities—Fund Restoration Alliance and Tax Support Circle—to solicit new funds and discourage litigation. These allegations center on distinct fraudulent schemes perpetrated outside the scope of the original investment relationship. Davidson’s liability arises from these specific, extra-contractual misrepresentations, not from the underlying container leasing agreement.

Permitting Davidson to enforce the arbitration clause would unjustly expand the scope of the original contract to cover unrelated future torts committed by a third party. Because the claims are not integral to or intertwined with the original contract terms, but rather stem from Davidson’s independent predatory conduct, he lacks standing to compel arbitration. Harper Investors are entitled to their day in court.

Harper Investors contracted with Gold Reserve & Lending, not Jon Davidson. As a non-signatory, Davidson lacks the standing to compel arbitration because Harper Investors never agreed to litigate disputes with him in a private forum.
